newsitem.title: UK: Britain's utilities tax takes election centre stage.
newsitem.headline: Britain's utilities tax takes election centre stage.

text.p: Opposition Labour Party plans for a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities became a key election issue on Tuesday as the campaign kicked off in earnest.

A day after Conservative Prime Minister John Major set May 1 as the election date, Labour reaffirmed its plans to raise at least three billion pounds ($4.8 billion) with a tax on what it sees as the excess profits racked up by utilities since privatisation.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke derided the scheme as damaging to the economy.
Labour's finance spokesman, Gordon Brown, said the windfall tax was a one-off levy which would be spent on helping the young and long-term unemployed into work.

"I've made that absolutely clear," he said. "We are utterly satisfied that the three billion pound employment programme that we are proposing and outlining today will be comfortably financed within the windfall levy."

The tax is one of the few economic proposals that differentiates the two main parties. Brown has already pledged to stick to Conservative spending plans for the next two years and leave key income tax rates unchanged.
Clarke used his news conference to accuse Labour of threatening the economic recovery.

"The windfall tax, which as I understand it is due to raise either three billion pounds or five billion pounds out of key British industries, is a serious threat to our continued recovery," he told reporters.
More bad news came the utilities' way on Tuesday as a report from parliament's Trade and Industry Select Committee said competition in electricity generation was not yet adequate.

The report did not tackle the idea of a windfall tax but in a conclusion likely to be seized upon by Labour, the all-party group of MPs said the the price control formula was set too low in order to make energy company flotations attractive.
"We are not yet convinced that sufficiently robust competition exists to guarantee that consumers will obtain the best possible prices," it said.
Brown declined to specify which companies would be hit by the windfall tax or say precisely how much money would be raised.
But a Labour spokesman said British Telecommunications Plc and BAA Plc, which runs the country's major airports, are likely to be hit by the tax, as well as electricity, gas and water suppliers.
Clarke said BT had done nothing to deserve a tax on profits.

"British Telecom is one of the most successful privatisations we've had," Clarke said. "To load the costs of a tax on British Telecoms is contrary to the interests of UK Ltd. It would damage our excellent economic performance."
He said Britain's modern telecommunications network was a key factor in attracting investment by overseas companies, particularly in financial services.
Clarke said the continuing problem of unemployment could not be dealt with by a one-off levy.

Since Brown first made his windfall tax pledge, 400,000 jobs had been created in Britain, Clarke said. "The real economy outperforms social democratic tax and spending schemes any day." ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
